Gill sets the parable among its predecessors, a siege drawn on a tile and a razor passed over the head, and adds this one: a fruitless vine fit only for burning. Clarke states the whole chapter in a line to the same effect. Keil and Delitzsch supply the argumentative link, and it is the chapter's key. The preceding word had destroyed the hope that a few righteous men might save the city; this one destroys the other prop, the fancy that election itself put the nation beyond rejection, by denying that it holds any superiority over the nations at all.

Calvin describes the temper being attacked. The people boasted of a free kindness as though it proved them excellent by nature, and used the very gifts they had been given as armour against the giver, so that sharp reproof was met by an inventory of privileges. The simile answers exactly that: whatever distinction they had was accidental and not intrinsic, conferred rather than possessed, so the argument from their own superiority collapses as soon as it is asked where the superiority came from.

Henry approaches it from the other side, as a correction of the prophet's own likely thoughts. Jerusalem was a noble structure and the joy of the whole earth, and its ruin a pity; and the answer comes as a comparison. A fruitful vine is as valuable as any tree there is, once invited in the old fable to reign over the rest, and its fruit gladdens God and man; the city had been planted as exactly such a choice vine, wholly a right seed, and had it borne fruit befitting a holy place it would have been the glory of both.

The question turns on what the wood is good for once the fruit is gone. Gill grants that the fruit is excellent and says the timber is worthless, and draws the moral that a people who owed everything to grace became, on degenerating, worse than any. Clarke concedes that in some countries the stock grows thick, but denies it is ever dense enough for furniture, and insists in any case that the branch is what is meant, than which he scarcely knows a more useless thing in any forest: nobody could make from it even a peg to drive into a mud wall, and nobody would grow a vine for its timber. Wesley puts it comparatively, that one branch off any forest tree is worth more than a whole vine except for what it bears. Gill runs through the trades that would have no use for it, carpenter, joiner, housewright and shipwright alike, and reports that a Roman naturalist knew of curiosities made from vine wood, though not of common articles and not from ordinary vines.

The burning finishes the argument, and Clarke turns the picture into a map. A branch thrown on the fire catches at both ends while the middle scorches, and so the extremities of the country were already wasted while the middle, the capital itself, stood under siege and would be destroyed in its turn. Gill and Wesley agree on the plain sense, that barrenness is what sends the wood to the fire. Gill also presses the closing question about the unburnt branch: before ever the flame touched it, when the nation was still whole and undeported, it would not have made so much as a peg; the charring only makes visible a uselessness that was there from the start.

Clarke states the application as an equation of certainties: as surely as such wood has been assigned to the fire, so surely have the inhabitants been assigned to be consumed. He also sums up the parable's purpose, which is to bring down a particular kind of pride — a people who in their best days had nothing but what was given them, and therefore deserved nothing, and who now, having lost even that character, have nothing to expect but judgment with no mercy mixed in.

Calvin reads the burning as already half accomplished, and makes the geography carry the argument. The outlying country had been wasted and the northern kingdom cut off altogether, so that the capital was left standing like the middle of a faggot with both ends alight; and the people, worn down by successive disasters, were exactly the charred stick of the figure. What astonishes him is that they went on defying a God who had humbled them by so many stages. He also disposes of two renderings offered for the branch. The wild vine he thinks simply impossible here, and the palm hardly better: a palm branch has no business among forest trees, since palms are not planted in woods among tall timber.

The threat of one fire after another is taken practically by Clarke. Escaping the sword leaves famine, escaping famine leaves deportation, and escape as such is not on offer; he reaches for the old proverb about running onto one hazard in the act of avoiding another, and for a homelier version of it, out of the scald into the flame.

Calvin explains why the sentence had to be repeated in that form. Because the city had not been reduced to dust it kept a kind of shape, and while a throne stood there the people kept a name, which was precisely what fed the obstinacy: men not wholly consumed concluded they would not be consumed at all. To that he adds a second folly, the habit of treating every reprieve as a deliverance — the besiegers withdrawing, no fresh army arriving, supplies failing the enemy — after which they not only breathed again but openly laughed at God and at the prophets, as men out of all danger. Against that he sets the force of the phrase about setting the face, which he says means persisting steadily rather than acting in passing, staying until the thing intended is done.

The last verse closes on the ground of it all. Gill describes a country left untilled with man and beast cut off. Clarke calls the offence prevarication and the offenders the worst of sinners, due the heaviest punishment, and asks whether men can really suppose that even their darkest thoughts are hidden. Wesley finds the same continuousness in the wording, an offending so unbroken that it reads as a single act.
